title: Top 10 Essential English Verbs for Absolute Beginners (A0–A1 / A2 Master Guide)
dek: A complete 12-page magazine spread for absolute beginners discovering English. Master the top 10 core verbs step-by-step, starting with a deep dive into the verb 'To Be' with full conjugations, 10 core usage patterns, negative/question structures, and real-world sentence frames.

blocks.text: Page 1: Introduction to the Top 10 Core Verbs

Welcome to Part 1 of our 2-part master verb guide for A0–A1 and A2 English learners! When you start learning English, you don't need thousands of words to start speaking. Frequency research demonstrates that just 10 core verbs carry up to 80% of daily spoken output. This 12-page issue gives every core verb its own dedicated page with clear grammar rules, practical sentence frames, real-world examples, and common traps to avoid.

🗺️ Interactive Verb Map: Part 1 Core Verbs

Flip through this issue page by page or jump directly to any verb spread:

Page 2: 1. To Be — Existence, identity, age, states, location.Page 3: 2. To Have — Possession, bodily states, routines.Page 4: 3. To Think — Opinions, thoughts, beliefs.Page 5: 4. To Know — Facts, familiarity, skills.Page 6: 5. To Like — Preferences, tastes, polite requests.Page 7: 6. To Want / Would Like — Desires, ordering, plans.Page 8: 7. To Go / Be Going To — Movement, travel, future.Page 9: 8. To Can (Modal) — Ability, requests, permission.Page 10: 9. To Eat — Meals, dining out, daily food.Page 11: 10. To Drink — Beverages, hydration, social drinks.Page 12: Outro & Practice — Language matrix & test tools.

📈 CEFR Verb Progression Roadmap

LevelCore Verb FocusCommunicative Capability

A1come, do, make, see, say, get, can, eat, drinkDaily routines, simple descriptions, origin, asking questions, ordering food.
A2take, give, know, think, feel, work, would likePreferences, past experiences, future plans, workplace tasks, opinions.
<hr>
Page 2: BE — The little verb that does almost everything ✨

🗺️ **Your learning route**  🟢 **A0–A1 · Start here:** identity, age, feelings, descriptions, place, time.  🔵 **A1–A2 · Build confidence:** negatives, questions, possession, *there is/are*, everyday expressions.  🟣 **A2+ · One step further:** *be* as a helping verb. Keep this page as a reference—you do not need to memorise everything at once.

Meet **be**: *am, is, are*. It helps you say who someone is, how someone feels, where something is, what something is like, and what time or weather it is. English often needs **be** where another language may use a different structure. 💡 The trick is to learn the pattern with the meaning, not just the words.
01 · The three shapes of BE 🧩

💡 **Pattern to remember:** the subject chooses the form: **I am**, **he/she/it is**, **you/we/they are**. Short forms are very common in conversation. Use full forms when you want emphasis or a more formal tone.
02 · Ten everyday jobs for BE 🌟
🟢 **A · Identity and names** — say who someone is or identify a thing.  **Pattern:** subject + be + noun/name.  *I’m Maya. He’s my brother, Leo. This is my new book.*
🟢 **B · Jobs and roles** — use *a/an* with a singular countable job.  *I’m an English teacher. She’s a doctor. He’s an IT specialist.*  ⚠️ Say **a doctor / an actor**, not *she is doctor*.
🟢 **C · Age** — English uses **be**, not *have*.  *I’m 20 (years old). My parents are 55. How old are you?*  🚦 **Not:** *I have 20 years.*  ✅ **Say:** *I’m 20.*
🟢 **D · Nationality and origin** — use a nationality adjective or *be from + place*.  *I’m French. He’s Spanish. We’re from Paris.*  🔎 Nationality describes a person; *from* tells you their origin.

🟢 **E · Descriptions and characteristics** — be + adjective.  *My friend is tall and funny. The cake is delicious. My room is clean today.*  💡 Adjectives do not take a plural **-s**: *They are happy*, not *they are happies*.

🟢 **F · Feelings and physical states** — say how someone feels or what state they are in.  *I’m happy to meet you. We’re hungry and thirsty. He’s tired today.*  🗣️ **Mini-dialogue:** “Are you okay?” “Yes, I’m fine, thanks.”

🟢 **G · Location and position** — be + place/preposition.  *I’m at home. She’s in the kitchen. The keys are on the table.*  📍 **Useful place words:** **in** the room · **on** the table · **under** the bed · **next to** the café · **behind** the house · **in front of** the school · **between** two shops · **near** the station · **at** work/school.

🟢 **H · Time, weather and dates** — English commonly uses **it is** for time and weather.  *It’s 11 o’clock. It’s cold and sunny. It’s Friday. Today is October 23.*  💡 For dates, you can also say *It’s October 23rd* (especially in American English) or *It’s the 23rd of October* (common in British English).

🔵 **I · Demonstratives and possession** — *this/that is* for one thing; *these/those are* for more than one.  *This is my bag. That is her sister. These are our books. Those are my parents.*  ⚖️ **Be vs have:** *This bag is mine* identifies the owner; *I have a car* says what I own.

🔵 **J · Material, measurements and numbers** — be can describe what something is made of, its price, size or distance.  *The table is made of wood. The ticket is €10. The station is two kilometres away. My room is four metres wide.*  🔎 In *is made of*, **be** is part of a passive structure—see “One step further” below.
03 · Make it negative 🚦
To make a negative, put **not after am/is/are**. You do not need *do* or *does*.
⚠️ **Two common traps**  • Say **I’m not** or **I am not**—standard English does not use *I amn’t*.  • ❌ *She doesn’t be happy.*  ✅ *She isn’t happy.*
04 · Ask yes/no questions ❓
Move **am/is/are** before the subject: **You are ready. → Are you ready?**
💡 **Short-answer rule:** in positive short answers, use the full form: ✅ *Yes, she is.*  ❌ *Yes, she’s.* Negative short answers can use contractions: *No, she isn’t.*
05 · Ask for the detail: WH- questions 🔎

✨ **Two questions that look similar—but do different jobs:**  • **What is your teacher like?** → asks about personality or characteristics: *She’s kind and funny.*  • **How is your grandfather?** → asks about health or well-being: *He’s fine, thanks.*
06 · Say that something exists: THERE IS / THERE ARE 🏡
Use **there is** for one thing and **there are** for more than one. It is a useful way to talk about what you can see or what is available.
🗣️ **In real life:** *Is there a bank near here?* · *There’s a café next to the station.* · *There are two free seats.*
07 · Small words, big meaning: fixed expressions 💬

items: **be right / be wrong** — *You’re right. I’m wrong.*
**be afraid of / be sure** — *She’s afraid of dogs. I’m sure it’s okay.*
**be interested in / be good at** — *He’s interested in music. She’s good at English.*
**be late / early / ready / busy / free** — *We’re late. Dinner is ready. I’m free tomorrow.*

blocks.text: 🔎 Notice the prepositions that belong with some expressions: **interested in**, **good at**, **afraid of**. Learn them as little word groups.
08 · One step further: BE can be a helping verb 🟣 A2+
So far, **be** has carried the main meaning: *She is happy.* Sometimes, **be** helps another part of the sentence instead. You can recognise these patterns now and learn them gradually.

rows: Helps form the present continuous: an action happening around now.
The table is made of wood.
Helps form the passive: the sentence focuses on the thing or action, not the doer.

blocks.text: ⚖️ **Compare:** *She is happy* = **be** describes her state. · *She is working* = **is** helps form the action verb *working*.
09 · Quick check 🎯

blocks.question: Choose the correct sentence about age and a job.
options: She has 25 years and is doctor.
She is 25 and she is a doctor.
She is 25 and she has doctor.
blocks.explanation: Use **be** for age and put **a/an** before a singular countable job: *She is 25. She is a doctor.*

blocks.question: Choose the correct positive short answer: “Is she at home?”
blocks.explanation: Positive short answers use the full form: *Yes, she is.*

blocks.question: Complete the sentence: “___ there any cafés near here?”
blocks.explanation: Use **are** with the plural noun *cafés*: *Are there any cafés near here?*

blocks.question: Which sentence describes an action happening around now?
blocks.explanation: In *He is working*, **is + working** forms the present continuous. In the other sentences, *is* describes a state or identity.

blocks.text: 🌱 **You do not have to master every pattern today.** Start by noticing **am / is / are**, then practise one use at a time. The more examples you meet, the more natural BE will feel.

💌 Your COSY journey

You can now say who you are. Next, discover how to talk about the people and things that are part of your life.

Next: HAVE 🎒 — My life, my family, my things →
Page 3: Verb 2 — "To Have" (have / has)

The verb **to have** is one of the most essential verbs in English. At A0–A1 level, you use it to talk about possessions, family, physical characteristics, food and drink, daily activities, and health conditions.

There are two essential present simple forms to learn first:
• **have** — I, you, we, they
• **has** — he, she, it
1. Forms & Conjugation Table (Present Simple)

rows: I have a phone. / You have a nice house. / We have two children. / They have a new car.
I don't have a car. / You don't have a pen. / We don't have time. / They don't have any pets.
Do I have time? / Do you have a question? / Do we have class today? / Do they have tickets?
He has a sister. / She has blue eyes. / It has four legs.
He doesn't have a job. / She doesn't have a brother. / It doesn't have a name.
Does he have a pet? / Does she have a car? / Does it have a camera?

blocks.text:
⚠️ **IMPORTANT CONJUGATION RULE:** Use **has** only with *he*, *she*, and *it* in positive present simple sentences.
• Correct: *She has a cat.*
• Incorrect: *She have a cat.*
2. Main Usages & Sentence Frames

items: **A. Possessions:** *I have a new laptop.* / *She has a red bicycle.* / *We have a big house in Paris.* / *They have a friendly dog.*
**B. Family & Relationships:** *I have two brothers.* / *She has a young daughter.* / *He has a big family.* / *We have many good friends.*
**C. Physical Characteristics:** *I have brown eyes.* / *She has long blonde hair.* / *He has a dark beard.* / *The cat has a long tail.*
**D. Things & Features:** *The apartment has three bedrooms.* / *The car has four doors.* / *My phone has a great camera.* / *The school has a large library.*
**E. Problems & Needs:** *I have a problem with my laptop.* / *She has a bad headache.* / *We have an urgent question.* / *He has a lot of work today.*
**F. Time & Availability:** *I have free time this afternoon.* / *We have an important meeting today.* / *She has an English lesson at 10 AM.* / *They have no money.*

**G. Food & Drink (Action Meaning):** *I have a delicious sandwich for lunch.* / *She has a cup of tea every morning.* / *We have breakfast at 8 o'clock.* / *They have dinner together at home.* (Here *have* means *eat* or *drink*).

blocks.text: 3. Negative Sentences (-) & The Base Verb Rule
To make negative sentences with *have*, use **don't have** or **doesn't have**.

rows: I don't have any money. / We don't have class today.
She doesn't have a brother. / My phone doesn't have a good camera.

blocks.text:
⚠️ **VERY IMPORTANT RULE:** After *doesn't*, always use the base form **have**, never *has*.
• Correct: *She doesn't have a car.*
• Incorrect: *She doesn't has a car.*
4. Yes/No Questions (?) & Short Answers

⚠️ **QUESTION RULE:** When you use *does*, the main verb returns to its basic infinitive form, **have**.
• Correct: *Does she have a cat?*
• Incorrect: *Does she has a cat?*
5. Wh- Questions with "Have"

items: **What:** *What do you have in your bag?* / *What do you have for breakfast?*
**Who:** *Who do you have in your family?*
**How many:** *How many brothers do you have?* / *How many bedrooms does the house have?*
**How much:** *How much money do you have?* / *How much time do we have?*
**What colour:** *What colour eyes does she have?*
**What kind:** *What kind of phone does he have?*

blocks.text: 6. "Have got" vs "Do/Does Have"
*Have got* is common in informal English (especially British English) for possession, family, and physical features.

rows: I have a car. / She has a cat.
I've got a car. / She's got a cat.
I don't have a dog. / She doesn't have a car.
I haven't got a dog. / She hasn't got a car.
Do you have a pet? / Does she have a car?
Have you got a pet? / Has she got a car?
Yes, I do. / No, she doesn't.
Yes, I have. / No, she hasn't.

blocks.text:
⚠️ **NEVER MIX THE TWO SYSTEMS:**
• Correct: *Does she have a car?* OR *Has she got a car?*
• Incorrect: *Does she have got a car?*
7. Everyday Expressions & Illnesses with "Have"

items: **Daily Activities & Routines:** *have breakfast / lunch / dinner*, *have a coffee*, *have a shower / bath*, *have a break*, *have a rest*, *have a party*, *have a good time*, *have a look*, *have a chat*, *have a holiday*.
**Illnesses & Physical Conditions:** *have a headache*, *have a stomachache*, *have a cold*, *have a fever*, *have a toothache*.

**Countable vs Uncountable (some / any):**
  • Affirmative (+): *I have some apples.* / *I have some water.*
  • Negative (-): *I don't have any apples.* / *I don't have any money.*
  • Question (?): *Do you have any questions?*

blocks.text: 8. Common Mistakes & Side-by-Side Comparisons

Contrast these key structures with 'to be' and 'to have':
• **State / Feeling:** *I am hungry.* (be + adjective)
• **Possession:** *I have a sandwich.* (have + noun)
• **Activity:** *I have breakfast at 8 AM.* (have + meal)
9. Check Your Understanding

blocks.question: Choose the correct negative form: 'She ___ a brother.'
blocks.explanation: After 'doesn't', the main verb always returns to its base form 'have'. 'She doesn't have a brother' is correct.

blocks.question: Which sentence correctly mixes 'have got' and 'do'?
options: Does she have got a car?
blocks.explanation: Never mix 'do/does' with 'got'. Use 'Has she got a car?' or 'Does she have a car?'

blocks.text: <hr>

💌 Your COSY journey

From who you are to what you have — little by little, your world gets bigger.

Page 4: Verb 3 — "To Think"
**To Think** allows you to express your opinion, share your thoughts, and ask others for their view.
Forms & Sentence Frames

items: **Present Simple Forms:** I/You/We/They **think** | He/She/It **thinks**.
**Expressing Opinions (I think that...):** *I think it is a good idea.* / *I think learning English is fun.* / *She thinks this movie is great.*
**Short Responses:** *I think so.* (I agree / I believe so) | *I don't think so.* (I disagree).
**Asking Opinions:** *What do you think about this idea?* / *What do you think of this film?*
**Key Collocations:** *think twice before deciding* (be careful), *think about the problem* (consider), *think of a solution* (have an opinion/idea).

blocks.text: <hr>
Page 5: Verb 4 — "To Know"
The verb **to know** is essential for talking about facts, information, people, places, skills, and things we understand. In our logical sequence: first we think, and then we know!

The primary present simple forms are:
• **know** — I, you, we, they
• **knows** — he, she, it
1. Forms & Conjugation Table (Present Simple)

rows: I know the answer. / You know my brother. / We know this city well. / They know the truth.
I don't know his name. / You don't know this place. / We don't know what to do. / They don't know anyone here.
Do I know you? / Do you know the way? / Do we know the rules? / Do they know the price?
He knows the teacher. / She knows the answer. / It knows the route.
He doesn't know my address. / She doesn't know the truth. / It doesn't know any tricks.
Does he know the time? / Does she know Peter? / Does it know where to go?

blocks.text:
⚠️ **IMPORTANT CONJUGATION RULE:** Add **-s** to *know* only with *he*, *she*, and *it* in affirmative sentences.
• Correct: *She knows the answer.*
• Incorrect: *She know the answer.*
2. Facts, Information & Embedded Question Words

items:
**A. Facts & Direct Information (Subject + know/knows + noun):**
  • *I know the correct answer to question 5.*
  • *She knows his full name and phone number.*
  • *He knows the truth about what happened.*
  • *We know the safety rules at work.*

**B. Information with Question Words:**
  • *I know where he lives in London.*
  • *She knows what you want for your birthday.*
  • *We know when the English lesson starts.*
  • *They know why he is angry today.*

blocks.text: 3. Familiarity with People & Places

items: **A. People:** *I know Anna from university.* / *She knows my older brother.* / *Do you know this man?* / *We don't know those people over there.*
**B. Places:** *I know this city very well.* / *He knows London like the back of his hand.* / *Do you know this Italian restaurant?* / *They don't know the area.*

⚠️ **DISTINCTION:** In English, *knowing someone* means you are familiar with them.
  • *I know Peter.* = I am familiar with him.
  • *I meet Peter every day.* = I encounter/see him every day.
  • *I know Peter well.* = I am very familiar with him.

blocks.text: 4. Negative Sentences (-) & "I don't know"

Use **don't know** or **doesn't know**. After *doesn't*, always use the base verb **know**, never *knows*.
• Correct: *He doesn't know.*
• Incorrect: *He doesn't knows.*

**The Essential Phrase — "I don't know":**
• "What's his name?" — "I don't know."
• "Where is my phone?" — "I don't know."
• **Useful Variations:** *I really don't know.* / *I don't know yet.* / *I don't know why.* / *I don't know anything about it.*
5. Yes/No & Wh- Questions (Embedded Word Order)

In embedded questions with *Do you know...?*, use **statement word order** (Subject + Verb).
• Direct question: *Where does he live?*
• Embedded question: *Do you know where he lives?* (Correct statement order: *where he lives*, NOT *where does he live*).
• *Do you know what time it is?* (NOT *what time is it*).
• *Do you know who she is?* (NOT *who is she*).
• *Do you know how old he is?* / *Do you know where the station is?*
6. "Know that" & "Know how to" (Skills)

items:
**A. Know (that) + sentence:** *I know that you are tired.* / *She knows that he is French.* / *We know English is important.* ('that' is optional in spoken English).
  • Negative contrast: *I don't know that he is here.* (lack of awareness) vs *I don't know if he is here.* (uncertainty).

**B. Skills (know how to + base verb):**
  • *I know how to swim.* / *She knows how to cook Italian food.* / *He knows how to drive a car.* / *They don't know how to play chess.*

**C. Know vs Know about:**
  • *I know Maria.* = I am acquainted with Maria personally.
  • *I know about computers.* = I have knowledge on the topic of computers.

blocks.text: 7. Stative Verb Rule & Comparisons

⚠️ **STATIVE VERB WARNING:** *Know* describes a mental state, so it is **not** used in continuous tenses (*-ing*).
• Correct: *I know the answer.*
• Incorrect: *I am knowing the answer.*
• To talk about gradual familiarity, say: *I am getting to know him.*
8. Key Daily Expressions with "Know"

items: **let someone know** = inform me (*Let me know when you arrive!*)
**get to know someone** = gradually become familiar (*I want to get to know you.*)
**as far as I know** = to my knowledge (*As far as I know, the café is open.*)
**know by heart** = memorize completely (*I know this poem by heart.*)
**know for sure** = be 100% certain (*I don't know for sure.*)

blocks.text: 9. Check Your Understanding

blocks.question: Which sentence has correct word order after 'Do you know...?'
options: Do you know where is the station?
Do you know where the station is?
Do you know where is station?
blocks.explanation: In embedded questions after 'Do you know...?', use normal statement word order: 'where the station is'.

blocks.question: Choose the correct skill structure: 'She knows ___ driving a car.'
blocks.explanation: For skills, use 'know how to + base verb': 'She knows how to drive a car.'

blocks.text: <hr>

💌 Your COSY journey

Now you can talk about what you know. Ready to share what you enjoy and love?

Page 6: Verb 5 — "To Like" ❤️

After learning *to be*, *to have*, *to think*, and *to know*, let's master **to like**! This is a very useful verb for talking about things you enjoy, your hobbies, food, music, people, and preferences.
1. Preference Scale: Love, Like, Dislike & Hate

items: ❤️ **Love (❤️❤️❤️❤️❤️):** Enjoy very much (*"I love chocolate!"*)
❤️ **Like (❤️❤️❤️):** Enjoy (*"I like chocolate."*)
👎 **Dislike (👎):** Not enjoy (*"I dislike chocolate."* — Note: *Dislike* sounds formal; in daily English, people usually say *"I don't like chocolate."*)
😠 **Hate (😠):** Dislike very strongly (*"I hate cold weather."* — Note: Be careful using *hate* with people, as it sounds harsh).

blocks.text: 2. Conjugation Table & The Third-Person Rule
**To like** is a regular verb. In the present simple, add **-s** for *he*, *she*, and *it*.

rows: I like music. / You like pizza. / We like traveling. / They like concerts.
I don't like coffee. / You don't like tea. / We don't like waiting. / They don't like noise.
Do I like this? / Do you like tea? / Do we like this movie? / Do they like cooking?
He likes sports. / She likes reading. / It likes milk.
He doesn't like cold weather. / She doesn't like cats. / It doesn't like water.
Does he like football? / Does she like dancing? / Does it like warmth?

blocks.text:
⚠️ **IMPORTANT RULE:** Add **-s** with *he*, *she*, and *it* in positive sentences.
• Correct: *She likes pizza.*
• Incorrect: *She like pizza.*

In negatives and questions, after *doesn't* or *does*, the main verb returns to base **like**:
• Correct: *She doesn't like tea.* / *Does he like football?*
• Incorrect: *She doesn't likes tea.* / *Does he likes football?*
3. What Can Come After "Like"?

items: **Pattern 1: Like + Noun:** *I like Italian food.* / *She likes dogs.* / *They like classical music.*
**Pattern 2: Like + Verb-ing:** *I like swimming in the morning.* / *He likes cooking pasta.* / *We like watching films.* (Emphasizes active enjoyment)
**Pattern 3: Like + to + Verb:** *I like to read before bed.* / *She likes to dance.* / *They like to travel in summer.* (Emphasizes habit or preference)

⚠️ **DISTINCTION:**
  • *I like coffee.* = I enjoy coffee generally.
  • *I'd like a coffee.* = I want a coffee now, politely. (*Would like* is covered on Page 7 with *To Want*!).

blocks.text: 4. Related Verbs: Love, Dislike & Hate

The same grammar rules apply to *love*, *dislike*, and *hate*:
• *I love my family.* / *She loves dancing.*
• *He dislikes waiting.* (Or naturally: *He doesn't like waiting.*)
• *My cat hates water.* / *They hate getting up early.*
5. Everyday Expressions & Stative Verb Rule

items: **Intensity:** *I really like it!* (A lot) | *I quite like it.* (To some degree) | *I don't like it very much.*
**Polite Neutrality:** *I don't mind.* (It is okay / no objection) | *It's not my cup of tea.* (Idiom: Not something I enjoy)
⚠️ **STATIVE VERB RULE:** *Like* describes a state or preference, so use present simple in standard English (*I like this song*, NOT *I'm liking this song*).

blocks.text: 6. Check Your Understanding

blocks.question: Choose the correct sentence:
blocks.explanation: With 'she', use 'doesn't' followed by the base verb 'like' without an -s.

blocks.question: What does 'I'd like a glass of water' mean?
options: I want a glass of water, politely.
blocks.explanation: 'I'd like' means 'I would like', which expresses a polite desire right now, not a general hobby.

blocks.text: <hr>

💌 Your COSY journey

You’ve moved from me, to my life, to my people, and now to what I love. That’s already a little more English for your real life. ✨

Page 7: Verb 6 — "To Want / Would Like"
**To Want** and **Would Like** express desires, intentions, and polite requests.
Forms & Sentence Frames

items: **Direct Desires (Want + Noun / Verb):** *I want a glass of cold water.* / *I want to learn English fluently.* / *Where do you want to go tonight?*
**Polite Standard (Would like + Noun / Verb):** *I would like to order lunch now, please.* / *She would like a fresh salad.*
**Negative Forms:** *I don't want to be late for class.* / *He doesn't want to go home yet.*
**Common Phrases:** *if you want to come*, *I want to know the truth*, *we would like to see the museum*.

blocks.text: <hr>
Page 8: Verb 7 — "To Go / Be Going To"
**To Go** expresses movement, travel, routines, and future intentions (*be going to*).
Forms & Sentence Frames

items: **Present Simple Forms:** I/You/We/They **go** | He/She/It **goes**.
**Movement & Prepositions:** *I go to work by train.* / *She goes to school every morning.* / *We go to the park on Sundays.*
**Exceptions without 'to':** *go home*, *go abroad on holiday*, *go downtown*, *go grocery shopping*.
**Future Intentions (be going to + verb):** *I am going to eat dinner with friends.* / *They are going to buy a new car next month.*
**Transport Phrases:** *go on foot* (walk), *go by bus*, *go by train*, *go by car*.

blocks.text: <hr>
Page 9: Verb 8 — "To Can" (Modal Verb)
**Can** is a modal verb expressing ability, permission, and polite requests.
Forms & Sentence Frames

items: **Modal Rule:** *Can* never changes form (no '-s' for he/she/it). It is followed directly by a base verb without 'to'.
**Ability:** *I can speak three languages.* / *She can swim very fast in the pool.* / *He can play the acoustic guitar.*
**Negative Ability (cannot / can't):** *I can't drive a manual car.* / *She can't come to the party tonight.*
**Requests & Permission:** *Can you help me with this bag?* / *Can I have a glass of water?* / *You can sit here near the window.*
**Useful Phrases:** *as fast as I can*, *I can do it*, *Can I ask a quick question?*

blocks.text: <hr>
Page 10: Verb 9 — "To Eat"
**To Eat** is used for food, daily meals, dining habits, and food preferences.
Forms & Sentence Frames

items: **Present Simple Forms:** I/You/We/They **eat** | He/She/It **eats**.
**Daily Food:** *I eat fresh fruit every morning for breakfast.* / *He eats lunch at 1 o'clock at work.*
**Questions & Desires:** *What do you want to eat for dinner?* / *Do you eat vegetarian food?*
**Phrasal Verbs & Collocations:** *eat out at an Italian restaurant*, *eat healthy food*, *let's find something to eat*.

blocks.text: <hr>
Page 11: Verb 10 — "To Drink"
**To Drink** covers beverages, hydration, offering drinks, and social café situations.
Forms & Sentence Frames

items: **Present Simple Forms:** I/You/We/They **drink** | He/She/It **drinks**.
**Daily Beverages:** *I drink two litres of water every day.* / *He drinks black coffee in the morning.* / *We drink hot tea in winter.*
**Offers & Polite Phrases:** *Would you like something to drink?* / *What would you like to drink with your meal?*
**Noun Usage:** *a hot drink on a cold day*, *a cold drink in summer*, *let's have a drink together*.
